The American renaissance. A flourishing of American arts and letters in the early-to-mid twentieth century, particularly centered in New York City. During this period, literature and visual art and theater and music achieved new prominence and innovation. New York emerged as a rival to European cultural capitals. The movement reflected America's rising economic and political power while fostering experiments in form and expression that defined modern culture.

This cultural flowering occurred roughly between the nineteen tens and nineteen forties, though its cultural effects persisted for decades. New York City served as the epicenter: home to publishers and galleries and theaters and cafes and magazines that fostered artistic collaboration and experimentation. The Harlem Renaissance was a concurrent and overlapping movement, producing major African American writers and musicians and visual artists.

American literature gained international stature through writers like F. Scott Fitzgerald and Ernest Hemingway and Sherwood Anderson, who adopted modernist techniques while exploring American themes. The period saw unprecedented exchange between American and European artists. Expatriates and migrants and traveling performers circulated ideas and forms across the Atlantic. Visual artists including Georgia O'Keeffe and the Ashcan School painters developed distinctly American aesthetic vocabularies. Theater flourished. Eugene O'Neill and others created serious American drama. Musicals emerged as a distinctive American art form.

Jazz and the blues and vernacular music achieved artistic legitimacy and international influence during this period, often celebrated alongside literature and visual art. The period ended symbolically with the Great Depression and World War Two, which redirected cultural attention and energy. New York City was the geographic and social center where the movement crystallized and thrived. American literature was the literary branch of the broader cultural flowering. The Harlem Renaissance was a concurrent and overlapping movement centered on African American artistic expression. Modernism provided the formal and philosophical framework underlying much American Renaissance work. Jazz was a musical form that rose to prominence and international recognition during the same period.
